name: Gilgamesh: A New Verse Translation
date: Liveright (W. W. Norton), New York, 14 April 2026, 224 pp., ISBN 9781631496684; Faber & Faber, London, UK edition 8 October 2026 (ISBN 9780571357246)
creator: Simon Armitage (UK Poet Laureate, professor of poetry at the University of Leeds), working with Oxford Assyriologist Jacob L. Dahl
form: Verse translation in loose four-beat lines, with short passages of justified prose for material outside the Standard Babylonian version, prose outlines heading each tablet, and about 40 pages of front matter (Introduction plus 'A Note on the Translation')
translator_access: Armitage does not read Akkadian. He worked from a translation of the cuneiform prepared by Jacob L. Dahl and read through a transliteration to get a feel for the sound (LARB, Nicolas Liney). He has said poetry should be left to poets and called Benjamin Foster's objection to non-Assyriologist translators 'disheartening and discouraging'. He first read the whole poem in Stephen Mitchell's 2004 version (Pittsburgh Review of Books interview).
scholarly_adviser: Jacob L. Dahl, Assyriologist, University of Oxford
versions_used: Built on Sîn-lēqi-unninni's twelve-tablet Standard Babylonian version, with gaps filled from other tablets (Old Babylonian and other non-standard sources) rendered in prose; front matter discusses recent finds such as the Sulaymaniyah Museum fragment of Tablet V (acquired 2011, about 20 new lines of Cedar Forest description). Whether the Sulaymaniyah lines are incorporated into the verse and which exact Old Babylonian or Sumerian witnesses are used is [uncertain]
non_standard_material: Marked typographically: material taken from tablets other than the Standard Version is set as brief blocks of justified prose rather than verse (Asymptote, Jordan Spector; LARB). This is the only distinct typographic device apart from the prose outlines at the start of each tablet.
gap_policy: Bridged, not displayed. Armitage writes that it is 'absolutely right to recognize the poem's inherent incompleteness' but not improper 'to favor readability and a sense of poetic wholeness over the worship of its accidental breakages.' He frames the work as 'a poem in a permanent state of evolution' and says 'All translation is an illusion. All translation is a compromise.'
typography_of_absence: No blank pages or rows of dots (contrast N. K. Sandars); lacunae are closed by justified prose summaries and continuous verse, so absence is largely invisible on the page. Brackets for broken signs are not reported by reviewers [uncertain]
tablet_xii: Unconfirmed [uncertain]. The OC Review of Books describes the book in terms of Sîn-lēqi-unninni's twelve tablets, but no review consulted says whether Tablet XII is translated in full, appended or dropped; LARB's account of the ending centres on the return to the walls of Uruk, suggesting the poem is read as closing at Tablet XI.
turning_point: Enkidu's death. Reviewers single out Gilgamesh watching over the body 'until a maggot falls from his nostril', which LARB calls 'a fantastically intense image that drives home death's finality'; in the Pittsburgh interview Armitage treats the death as what forces Gilgamesh into awareness of mortality and the doomed quest for immortality. The journey to Uta-napishti then ends in disappointment, and the return to the walls re-frames it [uncertain as to Armitage's own stated hinge]
arc_interpretation: Primarily grief and the fear of death: LARB (Liney) reads it with Rilke as 'das Epos der Todesfurcht', and Armitage's introduction says 'Thousands of years later death is no less bewildering to humankind.' Secondary strands: love between men (publisher copy; a Southern Bookseller Review blurb calls it 'proto-bromance', Asymptote reads the friendship through tragic-romance structure while noting Armitage treats a sexual reading as debatable), and a closing turn to community, since the final walls of Uruk loop back to the opening and place Gilgamesh within the city rather than alone (LARB). LARB also flags the Cedar Forest episode as an ecological and imperial problem for modern readers.
key_passages: Shamhat and Enkidu (restrained): 'She showed the wild beast the pleasures of a woman. / She made him want her, arousing his desire. / For six days and seven nights the two of them coupled' (quoted in LARB). Walls of Uruk (opening and close): 'Walk around on the upper walls of Uruk / inspect the stronghold's solid structure. / Aren't its courses composed of kiln-baked bricks?' (LARB). Enkidu's death: maggot falling from the nostril (LARB paraphrase). Death in the bedchamber, Tablet XI: 'death haunts my bed, stalks my chamber' (quoted in Asymptote). Siduri's advice: no review consulted quotes Armitage's rendering [uncertain]
diction_and_metre: Loose four-beat accentual lines, compact like the Akkadian, moving the narrative while 'lingering over each line' (LARB). 'Archaizing without being antiquated' (LARB); 'rhythmic contemporary English' (publisher). Keeps the source's verbatim repetition, e.g. the 23-line dream-journey block repeated five times in Tablet IV (OC Review of Books). Vivid concrete imagery: 'ramparts as straight as woolen thread', 'a savage young brute at home in the outlands'.
sample_line: "his voice is a raging torrent, / his mouth is the fire god, his breath is death" (Humbaba; quoted in Eric Bies, Orange County Review of Books, 19 April 2026)
critical_response: Strongly positive. William Giraldi, Wall Street Journal (24 April 2026): 'a reanimation, a voice tugged up from the clay and made to speak again', 'a poet's mastery of rhythm and rupture', 'an epic that breathes, raggedly, unevenly, but thrillingly alive'. Nicolas Liney, Los Angeles Review of Books: 'unhurried and resplendent, archaizing without being antiquated'. Eric Bies, Orange County Review of Books: 'our best, most lucid and fluent Gilgamesh to date', a classroom rival to Andrew George's Penguin. Jordan Spector, Asymptote (2 March 2026): 'Nobody owns Gilgamesh, because everybody owns Gilgamesh.' David Luhrssen, Shepherd Express: achieves 'a historically informed version that speaks to the widest readership'. Victor Mair reposted the WSJ praise on Language Log.
controversies: The poet-versus-Assyriologist question: Benjamin Foster (Yale) wrote in World Literature Today that he has 'no patience with clueless folk who think that they can translate the epic without going to the trouble of mastering Babylonian'; Armitage, who works from Dahl's crib, called this disheartening and argued poets should handle the poetry. A secondary liberty question is his choice to smooth over lacunae for readability. No provenance disputes reported.
regional_reception: No Arabic, Kurdish or Iraqi reception found; English-language (US/UK) release only as of September 2026 [uncertain]
ai_craft_tension: No machine involvement is reported; the book is a clean example of the older division of labour that AI now mimics. A specialist (Dahl) supplies the literal crib, the poet supplies rhythm, voice and wholeness, and the argument over whether that is legitimate (Foster vs Armitage) is the same one now raised about machine translation of cuneiform: who can claim a text they cannot read in the original. Armitage's defence ('All translation is an illusion. All translation is a compromise'; favouring 'poetic wholeness over the worship of its accidental breakages') marks what still needs a human: judgement about what to smooth, where to break into prose, and how a line should sound. His own nod to the Sulaymaniyah fragment shows new finds keep changing the base text he works on.
essay_hooks: (1) Armitage cannot read Akkadian and worked from Jacob Dahl's crib, yet the WSJ called the result 'a voice tugged up from the clay' (Giraldi, WSJ, April 2026). (2) Foster: 'no patience with clueless folk who think that they can translate the epic without going to the trouble of mastering Babylonian' (World Literature Today, via LARB). (3) 'the worship of its accidental breakages': Armitage's phrase for faithfully showing every gap. (4) No rows of dots: gaps become justified prose, a quiet typographic confession of repair (Asymptote). (5) 'All translation is an illusion. All translation is a compromise.' (Pittsburgh Review of Books). (6) Tablet IV repeats 23 lines five times, kept verbatim (OC Review of Books). (7) 'Nobody owns Gilgamesh, because everybody owns Gilgamesh' (Asymptote).
